title: Chapter I
focus: Nick, the Eggs and the Buchanans

teacherSummary.text: Nick Carraway, a Yale graduate from a well-off Midwestern family, explains that he came East in 1922 to learn the bond business and rented a small house in West Egg beside Gatsby's mansion. He dines across the bay in East Egg with his cousin Daisy, her husband Tom Buchanan (a former Yale football star with a 'cruel body') and the golfer Jordan Baker. Tom rants about a racist book; a phone call reveals that Tom has a mistress; Daisy tells Nick she hopes her daughter will be 'a beautiful little fool.' Back home, Nick sees Gatsby alone on his lawn, stretching his arms toward a green light across the water.

context.history: Great Neck and Manhasset Neck on Long Island's North Shore were home to new show-business fortunes and old society families in the early 1920s; Fitzgerald lived in Great Neck in 1922–24. After the First World War many young men from the Midwest moved east to work in finance, as Nick does.

significance: The opening establishes Nick as both guide and suspect witness, maps the novel's class geography (West Egg versus East Egg), and plants its key symbol, the green light.

I read “In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been turning over in my mind ever since” slowly and put it in my own words: The opening sentence: Nick presents himself as thoughtful and fair. Next, craft. I notice that the sentence moves in one steady line, which makes the statement sound settled and sure. The word “vulnerable” is the strongest in the line; it sharpens the picture more than a plainer word would. Then, effect. Whose eyes am I seeing through, and what might they miss? My answer: Nick introduces himself as a narrator "inclined to reserve all judgements," then judges everyone; the reader must weigh his claims.

segments.script: Annotate the chapter for point of view, setting (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this chapter suggest about Nick, the Eggs and the Buchanans? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Chapter I develops the idea of Nick, the Eggs and the Buchanans. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The first chapter sets up Nick as a narrator whose claims of fairness must be tested. When the text says “a single green light, minute and far away, that might have been the end of a dock” (Chapter I, paragraph 152), it shows this directly. He opens with his father's advice he has been "turning over in my mind ever since" and claims to reserve judgment, yet his portraits of Tom and Daisy are sharply judgmental, and he alone sees Gatsby reach toward "a single green light, minute and far away."

contentNotes.teacherNote: Tom praises a racist book about 'the Coloured Empires' and the dominance of 'the Nordic race.' Fitzgerald makes Tom look foolish, but elsewhere the narration itself reproduces racial and antisemitic stereotypes (Ch II, IV, VII, IX); students should be able to discuss both. Name the real 1920s pseudo-science Tom echoes. This section mentions drinking or a drug (“…ng-cake of the ceiling, and then rippled over the wine-coloured rug, making a shadow on it as…”). Treat it as period custom or plot detail; name it plainly and don't glamorize it.
